title: Account Access Removal
summary: Account Access Removal is the deliberate destruction of the accounts people need in order to work. The behaviour ranges from deleting a user, disabling an account or locking it out with failed attempts, to resetting a password, revoking a licence or stripping permissions in a hosted service so that the owner can no longer sign in. On Windows the net user utility, the Set-LocalUser and Set-ADAccountPassword commands in PowerShell, and Group Policy changes all produce this outcome, while on Linux the passwd tool changes credentials and ESXi hosts allow account changes through esxcli. Evidence is concentrated in identity logs: account management events on domain controllers and member servers, group policy change records, directory audit events in cloud identity providers, and service logs showing licence or permission changes. The signal that separates abuse from helpdesk work is scale, actor and timing, because a normal reset affects one account and arrives through a ticketing system, whereas destructive activity hits many privileged or service accounts in minutes and is frequently followed by a logoff or restart so the change cannot be reversed by the previous owner.

beginner.definition: This technique means taking away people's accounts so they cannot log in. An attacker may delete, lock or change an account. They may also remove permissions from a service such as a file sharing site.
beginner.whyItMatters: Accounts are the keys to almost every system. If they are removed, staff cannot work and responders cannot log in to fix things. It is often done just before files are encrypted. Restoring access can take days when the accounts themselves no longer exist.
howItWorks: First the attacker needs rights over accounts. These usually come from an administrator account they have taken over.
They pick the accounts that matter most, such as administrators, service accounts and support staff.
They delete, disable or lock those accounts, or reset the passwords so the real owners are shut out.
Some attackers prefer to keep the accounts and change permissions, for example removing a user from a shared site.
On hosted services they can also take away a licence, which quietly blocks the person from signing in.
They often force a logoff or restart afterwards, so the old sessions and cached rights are cleared.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the landlord replaces every door lock and then leaves. The tenants still live there, but their keys no longer work, so nobody can get in, and the building manager cannot reach the boiler room either. Later, when the tenants finally get new keys, some rooms have been emptied.
takeaways: Destroying accounts is an attack on availability and a common step before ransomware.
Keep at least one emergency administrator account that is not part of normal daily use, and test it.
Alert on sudden bursts of account deletion, disabling or password reset, especially on privileged accounts.

objectives: Describe the ways an account can be removed, disabled, locked or stripped of permissions.
Explain how account management events in identity logs reveal this behaviour.
Explain why attackers combine account removal with a logoff or system restart.
Distinguish a legitimate helpdesk account change from destructive bulk account removal.
Describe the recovery risk created when administrator accounts are deleted before systems are restored.
